claims.text: AlNbTiZr medium-entropy-alloy coatings with approximately 10 at.% Al can be deposited on zirconium-alloy cladding by RF magnetron co-sputtering.
An AlNbTiZr coating containing about 10 at.% Al has better corrosion resistance than otherwise comparable AlNbTiZr coatings with other Al contents.
The approximately 10 at.% Al coating forms a dense oxide scale containing Nb2Zr6O17 and ZrO2.
The dense oxide scale acts as a barrier to oxygen penetration into the zirconium-alloy substrate.
Optimizing the Al content promotes formation of a compact oxide layer, thereby improving corrosion or oxidation resistance.
The oxide layer formed by the optimized coating is adherent.
Inhibiting oxygen penetration will delay rapid oxidation during a LOCA-like high-temperature steam event.
The approximately 10 at.% Al coating will significantly reduce oxidation rates relative to uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding.
Under the proposed LOCA-like steam conditions, the coated cladding will have an oxide scale around 0.8 micrometers thick, compared with more than 3 micrometers on uncoated cladding.
The approximately 10 at.% Al coating will lower oxidation-induced weight gain relative to uncoated or non-optimized controls.
The coating and oxide layer will maintain structural integrity during high-temperature oxidation.
The coating will improve corrosion resistance relative to the uncoated zirconium-alloy substrate.
Non-optimized AlNbTiZr coatings have thicker oxide scales than the approximately 10 at.% Al coating.
The coating will retain suitability for nuclear-fuel-cladding service.
The hypothesis should hold in high-temperature steam oxidation conditions representative of a PWR LOCA.
A deposition temperature around 300 degrees Celsius and controlled pressure are suitable process conditions for making the proposed coating.
Performance under long-term neutron irradiation and after scale-up to full-size cladding remains unvalidated.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing coated and uncoated zirconium-alloy samples in the same LOCA-like steam exposure.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant reduction of at least 50% in both oxide-scale thickness and weight gain, or formation of a discontinuous non-dense oxide, would falsify the hypothesis.
